title_en: From Paris Student to Two Nobel Prizes
title_ru: От парижской студентки до двух Нобелевских премий
description_ru: Биография Марии Кюри: от бедной студентки в Париже до двух Нобелевских премий, открытия радия и помощи раненым на войне.
text:
Marie Curie is one of the few people in history who have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Yet her story did not begin with fame or money. She was born in Warsaw in 1867 as Maria Sklodowska, the youngest of five children. At that time Poland was not an independent country, and the Russian authorities controlled the schools. Women were not allowed to study at the university in Warsaw, so a talented girl like Maria had very few options.

Her parents were both teachers, and they believed strongly in education. However, the family lost most of its money, and her mother died when Maria was only ten. She finished school at the top of her class, but she could not go on to university. Instead, she made a deal with her older sister Bronya. Maria would work as a governess and pay for Bronya's medical studies in Paris, and later Bronya would help her in return. It was a hard bargain, and it took several years.

In 1891 Maria finally arrived in Paris and enrolled at the Sorbonne, where she changed her name to Marie. She was often cold and hungry in those years. She rented a tiny room on the top floor, and in winter the water in her jug sometimes froze overnight. Sometimes she ate nothing but bread and tea, and she once fainted in class. Even so, she passed her physics degree in 1893 with the highest marks, and a year later she completed a second degree in mathematics.

In 1894 she met a French physicist called Pierre Curie. They shared the same passion for research, and they married the following year. Their marriage was a real partnership. They worked side by side in a small, leaky shed that had once been used for medical dissections, and the building was so cold and damp that many scientists would have refused to enter it. Marie later remembered those years as the happiest of her life.

At that time scientists had just discovered that some materials give off mysterious rays. Marie decided to measure them carefully. She noticed that a mineral called pitchblende was more active than the uranium it contained, which meant that it must hold something else. In 1898 she and Pierre announced two new elements. They named the first one polonium, after her native country, and the second one radium. To prove that radium really existed, she had to process tons of ore by hand, stirring huge pots of boiling liquid for hours every day.

The effort was rewarded. In 1903 Marie, Pierre and the physicist Henri Becquerel shared the Nobel Prize in Physics, and Marie became the first woman ever to win the prize. Life seemed perfect, but in 1906 Pierre was killed in a street accident in Paris, when he slipped and fell under a horse-drawn cart. Marie was devastated. Nevertheless, she carried on with their work, and she took over his post at the Sorbonne, becoming the first woman to teach there.

In 1911 she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry, for her discovery of polonium and radium. No one had ever won two before. When the First World War began in 1914, she did not sit and wait. She designed small X-ray vehicles that could travel to the front line, and she trained women to operate them. People called the vehicles "little Curies". It has been estimated that more than a million wounded soldiers were examined with her equipment, and she even drove one of the cars herself.

Marie Curie also gave the world a new way of thinking about science. She did not take out a patent on the method of making radium, because she believed that knowledge should be shared. If she had sold it, she could have become very rich. Instead, she raised money for the Radium Institute in Paris, which still exists today as part of the Curie Institute and continues to fight cancer.

There was a terrible price to pay, however. Nobody realised at that time how dangerous radiation was. Marie carried tubes of radioactive material in her pockets and kept them in her desk drawer, because she loved the pale blue light that they gave off in the dark. She died in 1934 from a blood disease that was probably caused by years of exposure. Even now, her notebooks are so radioactive that they are kept in lead-lined boxes, and visitors must sign a form before they can read them.

Today Marie Curie is remembered as a brave, stubborn and generous scientist. She has inspired generations of young women to study science, and she has shown that if a person works hard enough, even the hardest obstacles can be overcome. Her life reminds us that great discoveries often come from patience, curiosity and a refusal to give up.

questions.question: Why could Maria not study at university in Warsaw?
questions.answer: Women were not allowed to study there, and the schools were controlled by the Russian authorities.

questions.question: What did Marie and Pierre Curie discover in 1898?
questions.answer: Two new elements: polonium and radium.

questions.question: How did Marie help during the First World War?
questions.answer: She designed small X-ray vehicles and trained women to operate them for wounded soldiers.

questions.question: Why did she not take out a patent on radium?
questions.answer: She believed that knowledge should be shared.
